title: 08. Multi-Agent & Patterns: Day 15 — Multi-Agent Systems
summary: By now you have built single-agent productivity tools in three frameworks. Today you graduate to multi-agent systems: graphs and pipelines where two or more specialized agents cooperate, each doing what it is best at.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
By now you have built single-agent productivity tools in three frameworks. Today you graduate to **multi-agent systems**: graphs and pipelines where two or more specialized agents cooperate, each doing what it is best at. The two big wins are (1) narrower prompts per agent (better accuracy, lower hallucination rate, easier testing), and (2) conditional control flow (one agent can ask another for help mid-task, which is impossible in a single linear prompt).

### Why split agents at all?

You might wonder: why not put research and writing in one giant system prompt? Three reasons. First, **cognitive scope**: a single agent asked to both research and write tends to do neither well — it conflates "what do I know" with "what should I say" and produces confident-sounding but shallow output. Splitting forces each agent to commit to one job. Second, **prompt evolution**: when the writer's output is unsatisfactory, you only need to tune the writer's prompt; the researcher's behavior stays stable. In a monolithic agent, every prompt change has unpredictable side effects. Third, **observability and cost**: a multi-agent graph emits per-node traces, so you can see exactly which agent failed. Per-agent token usage is also visible, which lets you swap cheaper models for simpler agents (e.g., use GPT-4o for the writer but GPT-4o-mini for the researcher).

The cost of splitting is **coordination overhead**: more code, more state to manage, more failure modes (especially infinite loops). Today's two projects expose the major coordination patterns you will reuse for the rest of the curriculum.

We will build two systems. The first is a **Researcher-Writer Duo** in LangGraph, where a writer agent can loop back to the researcher when its notes are too thin. The second is a **Triage-Respond Pipeline** in Pydantic AI, where a router agent exposes three responder agents as tools and delegates each incoming message to exactly one. The first demonstrates **graph-based coordination with cycles**; the second demonstrates **agent-as-tool composition**. Together they cover the two patterns that account for ~90% of real-world multi-agent designs.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
**Infinite loops in conditional edges.** Any `add_conditional_edges` that can return a node you have already visited needs a guard. In Project 1, `iteration < 3` prevents a writer that *always* asks for more research from looping forever. Always add a counter or a max-iterations check the first time you write a cyclic graph.

**State bloat via reducers.** The `Annotated[list[str], add]` reducer is wonderful but it accumulates forever. If your loop runs 10 times you will have 10 lists concatenated, and the writer's prompt will balloon. For long-running graphs, either cap the list size in the node (e.g., keep only the last 3 notes) or use a custom reducer that trims.

**Agent confusion in agent-as-tool.** When you expose Agent B as a tool to Agent A, Agent A's system prompt must explain *when* to call B and *what* B returns. Otherwise the router will hallucinate behavior or call multiple responder tools in one turn. Be explicit: "call exactly ONE responder tool" beats "use the responders to draft replies."

**Union output without a discriminator.** If you use `output_type=Union[A, B, C]` and none of A/B/C has a `Literal` field that distinguishes them, Pydantic will try each model left-to-right and may parse into the wrong one. Always add a `kind: Literal[...]` field on each branch of a Union output.
